tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find).

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size stays on that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane) until you call this tool again with preset "desktop", so reset it once you are done testing. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent, 5 touch points, and mouse-to-touch translation (hover stops producing hover states). Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

content.content:
# HW1 Spec Notes — "Building Your First Red-Black Tree in C"

**Source:** `CS370-HW1.pdf` (kept in this folder, not deleted — original stays as reference)
**Version:** 1.0, released 2026-08-25 · **Points:** 5 total
**One-line description:** Implement a red-black tree in C behind a frozen header, with airtight
memory management (verified by ASan/UBSan + valgrind), using Claude Code as a required,
disciplined collaborator — not a solve-it-for-me tool.

This is note #1 of 2 for this assignment. See [howto-notes.md](howto-notes.md) for the companion
walkthrough (the "how to work" document). This file covers the graded spec itself: what to build,
what's frozen, how it's graded, and the AI-usage rules that are actually enforced.

## The big picture / why this assignment is shaped this way

- This is **half of a two-assignment pair**. The tree built here gets reused, unmodified in spirit,
  in the *next* assignment — which adds custom allocators, injected allocation failures, and
  stack-limited (non-recursive) teardown. A near-twin of this tree later becomes part of the
  CPU scheduler in Assignment 4 (Linux's CFS runqueue uses a real red-black tree). **Nothing built
  here is throwaway** — build it to be understood, not just passed.
- Two intertwined goals: (1) a **systems goal** — correct, leak-free, double-free-free C — and
  (2) a **process-engineering-with-AI goal** — learn to direct Claude Code like a senior engineer
  directs a capable-but-overconfident junior.
- Explicit anti-goal: pasting the spec into Claude and saying "solve this." This actively hurts the
  grade (see Grading below) because of the process/transcript component and the live walkthrough.

## What is a Red-Black Tree (the actual CS content)

Five rules:
1. Every node is red or black.
2. The root is black.
3. Every missing child is conceptually a black sentinel leaf, `NIL`.
4. A red node has only black children (no two reds in a row on any path).
5. Every root-to-NIL path has the same number of black nodes = the **black-height**.

Consequence: height h ≤ 2·log₂(n+1), so search/insert/delete are all O(log n) worst case.

**Insertion** — new node always inserted **red** (keeps black-height unchanged everywhere; the only
possible damage is a red-red edge = a *local*, addressable violation).
- Fixup loop, red-uncle case: uncle is red → recolor parent+uncle black, grandparent red, then
  recheck two levels up. **No pointers move.** This can repeat — the violation just relocates
  upward; it is NOT guaranteed to finish in one pass.
- Key fact: **on the very first iteration of the fixup loop, a black uncle is always NIL** (a real
  black-with-subtrees uncle literally cannot occur yet — proven by a black-height counting
  argument). Rotation cases with substantial uncles only show up after the loop has already
  climbed once — meaning hand-testing with 5 keys will never exercise them; you need real
  volume (fuzzing) to hit rotation cases.
- When uncle is black: recoloring can't help. Need 1–2 rotations (zig-zag "kink" needs 2: one to
  straighten the shape, one to do the real repair + color swap). **Insert fixup never needs more
  than 2 rotations, total.**
- **Classic bug:** after a rotation moves the root to a new node, if your fixup only patches
  parent/child pointers and never updates `t->root`, `rb_find` starts silently searching a subtree
  and `rb_validate` will happily certify the (wrong) subtree as legal. Write a **stale-root
  regression test** the same day you write rotations.

**Deletion** — the unpleasant direction; damage is a *global count mismatch*, not a local violation.
- Removing a **red leaf** is free (no invariant impact).
- A node with **two children**: hoist the in-order successor's key+value into the doomed node's
  slot, then delete the successor instead (which has ≤1 child by construction). "Hoist" = transfer
  *ownership* of the key allocation — get this wrong and you get two nodes both believing they own
  the same key (→ double free at `rb_destroy` time).
- Every deletion funnels down to: **what happens when the physically unlinked node is black?**
  → creates a "doubly black" deficit — an **accounting fiction**, not a third color in the enum.
  The empty slot "owes" one black; fixup's job is paying that debt off by climbing toward the root.
- Deletion fixup case families (mirror images exist for all — don't forget them):
  - Sibling is black with no red children → recolor sibling red, debt moves up one level (if
    parent absorbs it by being red → turns black, done, no pointers moved — the "cheap" case,
    deletion's mirror of the red-uncle insert case).
  - Sibling has a red child → rotation drags that red across to the deficient side.
  - Sibling itself is red → rotate first just to reach a shape you already know how to handle.
  - Debt reaching the root just dissolves there (every path lost the same one black — equality
    restored, absolute black-height may drop by one, which is fine).
  - **Special/easy corner case:** deleting a black node with exactly one child. That child is
    *provably* red (proof by counting — a black child there would already have broken the tree
    before you touched it). Fix: splice the red child into the vacant slot, paint it black. Done —
    no debt, no fixup loop at all. **If your code launches the full sibling case analysis here,
    something is wrong** — this must be tested explicitly (spec calls out adding this exact case
    to the required table-driven tests).
- **Memory-safety tripwire repeated multiple times in the spec:** fixup must NEVER dereference
  freed memory. Either save everything you need (parent/sibling/slot info) *before* calling
  `free()` on the removed node, or restructure to free *after* fixup completes. Either order is
  fine; the ordering violation is not.

## From Java to C (field guide) — the two questions that matter for every pointer

For every pointer-like thing in this assignment, ask: **(1) how long does the pointee live, and
(2) who is responsible for eventually freeing it?** Java answered both silently; C answers neither.

- Pointer ≠ object. Copying a pointer copies an address, not the thing at that address (aliasing
  works like Java references — two names, one object — but *ownership* is a separate concept from
  *reachability*: many pointers can reach an object; exactly one owns it).
- `malloc(n)` gives raw, uninitialized, unconstructed bytes — nothing more. `free(p)` exactly once,
  never touch that pointer again after.
- Named failure modes: **leak** (never freed), **double free** (freed twice — corrupts allocator
  bookkeeping), **use-after-free** (freed then still used — "the most treacherous," because it
  often *keeps working* for a while).
- Local/stack variables die when their function returns — anything that must outlive the call
  (every tree node, every private key copy) needs heap storage via `malloc`.
- `malloc` **can return NULL** — must check every allocation. Partial-failure cleanup matters: if
  node alloc succeeds but the subsequent key-copy alloc fails, the first allocation is still yours
  to free ("the second malloc failed" is not an exemption from cleaning up the first).
- C strings are `char*` arrays terminated by `'\0'`. `==` on two strings compares **addresses**, not
  contents (bug you'll write once, remember forever) — use `strcmp(a,b) == 0`. Copying a string
  means `malloc(strlen(s) + 1)` — **never forget the +1** for the terminator.
- One logical tree node = **two separate heap allocations** (the node struct itself, and its private
  heap copy of the key string) — both must be tracked and freed, not just one.
- `struct` = fields only, no methods/constructors — `malloc`ing one gives raw bytes; you initialize
  every field yourself. Idiom: `malloc(sizeof *n)` — ties the allocation size to the pointer's type
  automatically.
- The public header uses an **opaque type** (`typedef struct rbtree rbtree_t;` with no visible
  fields) — C's version of "private," enforced by the compiler simply never being told the layout.
- A `parent` pointer is optional but common — makes fixup loops easier to write (classic textbook
  algorithms assume one), at the cost of one more pointer to keep correct through every rotation.
  **This is flagged as "your first real design decision."**

## Ownership contract (the actual grading contract — read like a lease)

- `rb_insert`: **on success**, the tree takes ownership of `value` (caller must never free it — the
  tree will, via `value_free`, when appropriate). **On failure** (`-1`), ownership never transferred
  — caller still owns `value` and must handle it. **On overwrite** of an existing key, the tree
  frees the *old* value before installing the new one (tree is the old value's only owner at that
  moment).
- Track three things separately per node: the node allocation, the tree's private key copy, and the
  opaque `value` (whose ownership follows the API rules above — not tied to node/key lifetime).
- Rotations change **topology only** — they never change who owns a node/key/value.

## Frozen API (`include/rbtree.h`) — NEVER MODIFY

```c
rbtree_t *rb_create(rb_value_free_fn value_free);      // NULL on alloc failure; value_free may be NULL
int       rb_insert(rbtree_t *t, const char *key, void *value); // 0 ok, -1 on alloc failure (unchanged, value NOT consumed)
void     *rb_find(const rbtree_t *t, const char *key);          // tree retains ownership
int       rb_delete(rbtree_t *t, const char *key);              // 0 ok, -1 if absent; frees key copy + value
size_t    rb_size(const rbtree_t *t);
void      rb_foreach(const rbtree_t *t, void (*fn)(const char*, void*, void*), void *ctx); // in-order
int       rb_validate(const rbtree_t *t);                       // 0 iff all invariants hold
void      rb_destroy(rbtree_t *t);                               // frees everything, NULL-safe
```
Keys are C strings, copied and owned by the tree. Values are opaque `void *`.

## Milestones (M0–M3 + optional Reach)

| Milestone | What | Est. hours |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | Setup: repo, `CLAUDE.md`, toolchain | 1 |
| M1 | Skeleton, insert (+rebalance), find, foreach, validate | 3–4 |
| M2 | Delete (all fixup cases) + fuzzer (≥10⁵ ops), green under asan+memcheck | 3–4 |
| M3 | Hardening, edge cases, final clean sweep | 1–2 |
| The Reach (ungraded) | Teardown *without recursion* — O(1) aux space via right-spine trick | 1–2 |
| — | Process artifacts (CLAUDE.md, PROMPTLOG.md, REFLECTION.md), written throughout | 1 |

**Discipline point emphasized repeatedly:** don't debug delete on top of an insert you don't trust
yet — "less a milestone than an archaeological dig."

### Required operations & testing bar
- Required: `rb_create`, `rb_insert` (w/ rebalancing), `rb_find`, `rb_delete` (full fixup, all
  cases), `rb_size`, `rb_foreach` (in-order), `rb_validate`, `rb_destroy`.
- `rb_validate` must check all 5 invariants + that `rb_size` matches actual node count.
- **Fuzzer:** ≥ 10⁵ random insert/find/delete ops vs. a reference model (sorted array or linked
  list is fine), calling `rb_validate` at least every 100 ops, under both asan and memcheck.
- **Targeted deletion tests are required in addition to fuzzing** (fuzzing alone won't reliably hit
  rare fixup shapes): minimum a red leaf, a black leaf with a red sibling, a two-children node,
  root deletion — **plus the black-node-with-one-red-child case** the spec adds explicitly. Each
  test must assert `rb_validate` and `rb_size` afterward.
- **Recursion is allowed** in `rb_destroy`/`rb_foreach` *for this assignment only* — the next
  assignment revokes it (stack-limited kernel-style constraints).
- **Tip explicitly recommended:** route all allocation through 4-line wrapper functions
  `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` (just forwarding to malloc/free for now) — this is the "seam" the *next*
  assignment's fault-injection harness will need. Install now, "while the house is small."

## Toolchain / verification requirements

- Must compile clean: `gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror`.
- `make asan` — AddressSanitizer + UBSan (compiled-in instrumentation; fast, pinpoints the exact
  bad instruction).
- `make memcheck` — valgrind (external, no rebuild needed, catches some uninitialized-read cases
  ASan misses; much slower). Required together — "belt and suspenders," deliberately redundant.
- **Hard rule: a single leaked byte, invalid read/write, or UB report caps that milestone's
  correctness score at 50%.** Not a warning — a failure, mechanically enforced.

## Deliverables (submitted as a tar via Canvas)

- Source: Makefile, `src/rbtree.c`, tests, the **unmodified** frozen `include/rbtree.h`.
- `CLAUDE.md` — checked in, evolving across milestones.
- `PROMPTLOG.md` — **4–6 annotated episodes** (prompt + response + your judgment: accepted /
  rejected / pushed back, and why). Must include at minimum: one plan you revised, one
  rejected/oversized diff, one tool-output debugging loop, one review finding you triaged.
  **Raw transcript dumps score nothing here — annotation is the actual deliverable.**
- `REFLECTION.md` (~1 page): where the agent was most/least reliable; one bug it introduced that
  you caught and how; what most surprised "the Java programmer you were two weeks ago."
- **Raw Claude Code session transcripts** (`.jsonl` files, unmodified, not exported/retyped) —
  found locally at `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl`. **These auto-purge after 30
  days** — copy them out periodically; losing them is not a valid excuse.
- Git history with **≥ 8 meaningful commits** tracking milestones — a single "final submission"
  commit is an **automatic process-grade of zero**.

## Grading breakdown (5 points total)

| Component | Method | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Core tree (insert/find/foreach/validate) | Unit tests + fuzzer (≥10⁵ ops) under asan+memcheck | 1.5 |
| Deletion, all fixup cases | Table-driven case tests + fuzzer w/ deletes green | 1.5 |

**Source:** `CS370-HW1.pdf` (kept in this folder, not deleted — original stays as reference)
**Version:** 1.0, released 2026-08-25 · **Points:** 5 total
**One-line description:** Implement a red-black tree in C behind a frozen header, with airtight
memory management (verified by ASan/UBSan + valgrind), using Claude Code as a required,
disciplined collaborator — not a solve-it-for-me tool.

This is note #1 of 2 for this assignment. See [howto-notes.md](howto-notes.md) for the companion
walkthrough (the "how to work" document). This file covers the graded spec itself: what to build,
what's frozen, how it's graded, and the AI-usage rules that are actually enforced.

## The big picture / why this assignment is shaped this way

- This is **half of a two-assignment pair**. The tree built here gets reused, unmodified in spirit,
  in the *next* assignment — which adds custom allocators, injected allocation failures, and
  stack-limited (non-recursive) teardown. A near-twin of this tree later becomes part of the
  CPU scheduler in Assignment 4 (Linux's CFS runqueue uses a real red-black tree). **Nothing built
  here is throwaway** — build it to be understood, not just passed.
- Two intertwined goals: (1) a **systems goal** — correct, leak-free, double-free-free C — and
  (2) a **process-engineering-with-AI goal** — learn to direct Claude Code like a senior engineer
  directs a capable-but-overconfident junior.
- Explicit anti-goal: pasting the spec into Claude and saying "solve this." This actively hurts the
  grade (see Grading below) because of the process/transcript component and the live walkthrough.

## What is a Red-Black Tree (the actual CS content)

Five rules:
1. Every node is red or black.
2. The root is black.
3. Every missing child is conceptually a black sentinel leaf, `NIL`.
4. A red node has only black children (no two reds in a row on any path).
5. Every root-to-NIL path has the same number of black nodes = the **black-height**.

Consequence: height h ≤ 2·log₂(n+1), so search/insert/delete are all O(log n) worst case.

**Insertion** — new node always inserted **red** (keeps black-height unchanged everywhere; the only
possible damage is a red-red edge = a *local*, addressable violation).
- Fixup loop, red-uncle case: uncle is red → recolor parent+uncle black, grandparent red, then
  recheck two levels up. **No pointers move.** This can repeat — the violation just relocates
  upward; it is NOT guaranteed to finish in one pass.
- Key fact: **on the very first iteration of the fixup loop, a black uncle is always NIL** (a real
  black-with-subtrees uncle literally cannot occur yet — proven by a black-height counting
  argument). Rotation cases with substantial uncles only show up after the loop has already
  climbed once — meaning hand-testing with 5 keys will never exercise them; you need real
  volume (fuzzing) to hit rotation cases.
- When uncle is black: recoloring can't help. Need 1–2 rotations (zig-zag "kink" needs 2: one to
  straighten the shape, one to do the real repair + color swap). **Insert fixup never needs more
  than 2 rotations, total.**
- **Classic bug:** after a rotation moves the root to a new node, if your fixup only patches
  parent/child pointers and never updates `t->root`, `rb_find` starts silently searching a subtree
  and `rb_validate` will happily certify the (wrong) subtree as legal. Write a **stale-root
  regression test** the same day you write rotations.

**Deletion** — the unpleasant direction; damage is a *global count mismatch*, not a local violation.
- Removing a **red leaf** is free (no invariant impact).
- A node with **two children**: hoist the in-order successor's key+value into the doomed node's
  slot, then delete the successor instead (which has ≤1 child by construction). "Hoist" = transfer
  *ownership* of the key allocation — get this wrong and you get two nodes both believing they own
  the same key (→ double free at `rb_destroy` time).
- Every deletion funnels down to: **what happens when the physically unlinked node is black?**
  → creates a "doubly black" deficit — an **accounting fiction**, not a third color in the enum.
  The empty slot "owes" one black; fixup's job is paying that debt off by climbing toward the root.
- Deletion fixup case families (mirror images exist for all — don't forget them):
  - Sibling is black with no red children → recolor sibling red, debt moves up one level (if
    parent absorbs it by being red → turns black, done, no pointers moved — the "cheap" case,
    deletion's mirror of the red-uncle insert case).
  - Sibling has a red child → rotation drags that red across to the deficient side.
  - Sibling itself is red → rotate first just to reach a shape you already know how to handle.
  - Debt reaching the root just dissolves there (every path lost the same one black — equality
    restored, absolute black-height may drop by one, which is fine).
  - **Special/easy corner case:** deleting a black node with exactly one child. That child is
    *provably* red (proof by counting — a black child there would already have broken the tree
    before you touched it). Fix: splice the red child into the vacant slot, paint it black. Done —
    no debt, no fixup loop at all. **If your code launches the full sibling case analysis here,
    something is wrong** — this must be tested explicitly (spec calls out adding this exact case
    to the required table-driven tests).
- **Memory-safety tripwire repeated multiple times in the spec:** fixup must NEVER dereference
  freed memory. Either save everything you need (parent/sibling/slot info) *before* calling
  `free()` on the removed node, or restructure to free *after* fixup completes. Either order is
  fine; the ordering violation is not.

## From Java to C (field guide) — the two questions that matter for every pointer

For every pointer-like thing in this assignment, ask: **(1) how long does the pointee live, and
(2) who is responsible for eventually freeing it?** Java answered both silently; C answers neither.

- Pointer ≠ object. Copying a pointer copies an address, not the thing at that address (aliasing
  works like Java references — two names, one object — but *ownership* is a separate concept from
  *reachability*: many pointers can reach an object; exactly one owns it).
- `malloc(n)` gives raw, uninitialized, unconstructed bytes — nothing more. `free(p)` exactly once,
  never touch that pointer again after.
- Named failure modes: **leak** (never freed), **double free** (freed twice — corrupts allocator
  bookkeeping), **use-after-free** (freed then still used — "the most treacherous," because it
  often *keeps working* for a while).
- Local/stack variables die when their function returns — anything that must outlive the call
  (every tree node, every private key copy) needs heap storage via `malloc`.
- `malloc` **can return NULL** — must check every allocation. Partial-failure cleanup matters: if
  node alloc succeeds but the subsequent key-copy alloc fails, the first allocation is still yours
  to free ("the second malloc failed" is not an exemption from cleaning up the first).
- C strings are `char*` arrays terminated by `'\0'`. `==` on two strings compares **addresses**, not
  contents (bug you'll write once, remember forever) — use `strcmp(a,b) == 0`. Copying a string
  means `malloc(strlen(s) + 1)` — **never forget the +1** for the terminator.
- One logical tree node = **two separate heap allocations** (the node struct itself, and its private
  heap copy of the key string) — both must be tracked and freed, not just one.
- `struct` = fields only, no methods/constructors — `malloc`ing one gives raw bytes; you initialize
  every field yourself. Idiom: `malloc(sizeof *n)` — ties the allocation size to the pointer's type
  automatically.
- The public header uses an **opaque type** (`typedef struct rbtree rbtree_t;` with no visible
  fields) — C's version of "private," enforced by the compiler simply never being told the layout.
- A `parent` pointer is optional but common — makes fixup loops easier to write (classic textbook
  algorithms assume one), at the cost of one more pointer to keep correct through every rotation.

rbtree_t *rb_create(rb_value_free_fn value_free);      // NULL on alloc failure; value_free may be NULL
int       rb_insert(rbtree_t *t, const char *key, void *value); // 0 ok, -1 on alloc failure (unchanged, value NOT consumed)
void     *rb_find(const rbtree_t *t, const char *key);          // tree retains ownership
int       rb_delete(rbtree_t *t, const char *key);              // 0 ok, -1 if absent; frees key copy + value

int       rb_validate(const rbtree_t *t);                       // 0 iff all invariants hold
void      rb_destroy(rbtree_t *t);                               // frees everything, NULL-safe

Keys are C strings, copied and owned by the tree. Values are opaque `void *`.

# HW1 Companion Notes — "The Companion: A Walkthrough for Building Your First Red-Black Tree with Claude Code"

**Source:** `CS370-HW1-HowTo.pdf` (kept in this folder, not deleted — original stays as reference)
**Version:** 1.0, released 2026-08-25
**Relationship to the spec:** this document never overrides [spec-notes.md](spec-notes.md) — where
they'd seem to disagree, the spec wins. This is the "how to spend your hours and tokens" companion,
not a second set of requirements.

## Purpose

Not required reading for the grade directly, but the professor states the students who land at the
top of the transcript rubric mostly work this way whether or not anyone told them to. It's organized
around: read → plan → build across two weeks, with commit/test/debug/write-down habits threaded
through. The token-discipline section is explicitly framed as "mostly a summary of habits you'll have
already picked up for other reasons" — i.e., good engineering practice and frugal token usage are
the same behavior, not a tradeoff.

## Glossary — terms worth having internalized (grouped by theme)

**Testing/tools:** *green* (everything passed) / *red* (something failed) · *the battery* (`make
test` → `make asan` → `make memcheck` run back to back) · *table-driven test* (one array of cases +
one loop; add a case by adding a row) · *repro* (exact recipe that reproduces a bug deterministically
— without one you have "a rumor, not a bug report") · *shrink/minimize* (cut a repro down to the
smallest failing case) · *seed* (fixes a fuzzer's "randomness" so failures reproduce) · *fuzzer* /
*reference model* (a dumb, trusted second implementation — e.g. sorted array — to compare against)
· *harness* (the scaffolding that sets up/runs/checks/cleans up a test).

**Code:** *slice* (one small piece of work finishable+testable+committable in one sitting — not a
"feature," not a "milestone") · *diff* (read every one, especially test-file diffs, before
committing) · *seam* (a boundary you can swap something in behind — `rb_malloc` is the seam this
assignment tips you to install for next month's fault injector) · *stub* (an honest do-nothing
placeholder that compiles) · *invariant* (always-true-at-loop-top; state it, and termination often
falls out) · *fixup* (the repair walk after insert/delete) · *doubly black* (deletion's accounting
fiction — lives in your reasoning, not your color enum) · *mirror case* (left/right swapped version
of a fixup case — "the half people forget to write. Or test.") · *ownership* (who eventually frees
an allocation — distinct from reachability) · *unwind* (undo partial work when something fails
halfway) · *teardown* (destroying the whole structure, distinct from single-key deletion) ·
*spelunking* (what the agent does, at your expense, when you don't tell it where to look).

**Git:** *commit* / *commit at green* (only snapshot working states) · `git restore` (free, instant
undo of uncommitted changes — vastly cheaper than paying an agent to un-write its own work) ·
`git bisect` (binary-searches history for a breaking commit — useless with one "final" commit) ·
*clean clone* (clone your own repo fresh and build from that — catches "only compiles because of an
untracked file" problems before submission).

**Agent/meter:** *token* (~4 chars of English prose, ~3 chars of C source — punctuation counts) ·
*context* (everything the model re-reads every single turn: prompt, `CLAUDE.md`, every opened file,
every command's output, all prior replies — "not a purchase, a subscription") · *context window*
(container size) vs. *usage limit* (your budget — you can be far from filling the window and still
be broke) · *session* (one conversation until `/clear`) · `/clear` (wipes conversation, `CLAUDE.md`
survives) · `/compact` (summarizes and continues — steerable: "keep the failing test output and the
current diff") · *plan mode* (Shift+Tab — agent reads/analyzes, cannot edit; "arguments are cheap
and mistakes cost nothing" here) · `CLAUDE.md` (loads every session — every line is a recurring
charge, keep it lean) · *slash command* (saved prompt, one keystroke, lives in
`.claude/commands/`) · *adversarial review* (fresh session attacks code it didn't write — avoids
the author's own blind spots) · *devlog* (`DEVLOG.md` — "memory that never once sends you a bill").

## Reading the spec itself (this section is about HOW to read it)

- **Pass 1 (45 min, no keyboard):** read for shape and tone only. Where the spec spends six figures

Concrete meaning of "commit wisely": one logical change per commit · commit only from green ·
commit *before* anything risky (so `git restore` — free — is available instead of paying tokens to
have Claude un-write its own recent work, "the saddest line item in this course") · read every
diff before blessing it, test diffs especially (catches the agent quietly weakening a test to make
it pass) · let Claude drive git *conversationally* only after you've already read the diff.

A sample healthy commit log is given (~15 lines from `M0: repo skeleton...` through
`docs: PROMPTLOG episodes 1-5 annotated...`) — useful as a template for what "8+ meaningful
commits" actually looks like in practice, not just in count.

## Testing as a ladder, not a ceremony

Climb one rung per slice, never all-at-once at the end ("the end is where testing goes to become
debugging"):
1. Unit tests born alongside each operation (same evening, not "when the tree is done").
2. `rb_validate` after every mutation inside tests — "the cheapest oracle you own." A bug caught one
   op later is a 5-minute fix; caught 4,000 ops later is an afternoon.
3. Table-driven cases *before* the hard code exists, especially for deletion — a first-draft
   `delete_fixup` will often pass random fuzzing while still failing a targeted case it just never
   randomly encountered.
4. Fuzzer vs. reference model, fixed seeds. On failure: **shrink before you prompt** — a 12-op
   repro is cheap for Claude to debug; a 100,000-op haystack is expensive, "and only one of those
   bills is worth paying."
5. Edge cases nobody fuzzes into by accident: empty tree, single node, overwrite-only-key.

Cadence: `make test` constantly (seconds) · `make asan` after each meaningful change · `make
memcheck` once per evening as a closing ritual (slow — let it be slow at the end, "like dessert").
Two standing rules: **never accept "the tests should pass now"** without real tool output; and
**watch for tests quietly getting weaker** (loosened assertions, vanished cases, thresholds drifting
down) — this is named as a real failure mode of real agents, and your own eyes on every test diff
are the actual enforcement mechanism.

The "10:40pm shrug" prompt is explicitly named as failing on both cost *and* effectiveness — it
forces the agent to read everything to answer anything, and a confident multi-file guess-diff
arrives that still has to be reviewed (the work you were trying to skip, just bigger).

Correct loop, in order: **(1) reproduce deterministically** (same seed → same failure every time;
if it won't reproduce, that *is* the bug report — in this assignment nondeterminism almost always
means a read of uninitialized memory or a use-after-free) → **(2) minimize/shrink** the failing
input → **(3) localize** with ASan/valgrind's file+line+backtrace → **(4) prompt scoped to the
module**, naming the file/function, pasting only the relevant tool-output lines (e.g. `grep -A6
'definitely lost'`) → **(5) smallest diff, verify with the same tool, commit, log the episode in
`PROMPTLOG.md` while it's warm**.

**Why brute force ("try again") structurally cannot converge:** every failed attempt stays in
context (cost climbs every turn while progress doesn't) · "try again" adds zero new information ·
the failed attempts become *misleading evidence* the model then conditions on (you're building a
case for the wrong theory) · the code itself degrades underneath you across repeated blind edits.
The exit is unglamorous: Escape, `git restore` to last green, get a deterministic repro, shrink it,
come back with a smaller question and a file name.

## Token/cost mental model (the "why" behind all the above habits)

- A token ≈ 4 chars of English prose, ≈ 3 chars of C source (denser punctuation/identifiers).
- **Input** = everything read (prompt + `CLAUDE.md` + opened files + command output + prior
  replies) — re-sent and re-billed on *every single turn* of a session, not once. "One big file
  read on turn 3 is a purchase. The same file still sitting in context on turn 30 is a
  subscription." **Output** is pricier per-token but input is where volume lives.
- Context window (container size) ≠ usage limit (your budget) — you can be far from filling the
  window and still be out of allowance.
- Two concrete cost scenarios worked out with real numbers: (a) pasting the whole spec into a
  session costs ~30k tokens once, but then gets re-billed on every subsequent message all
  evening — "you paid a fortune to make the answer slightly worse," since it's competing with your
  actual question for the model's attention; (b) "I have a leak, fix it" (~80k tokens/turn,
  compounding, confident 300-line multi-file diff to review) vs. the scoped version from the
  debugging-loop section (~2k tokens/turn, 15-line fix) — roughly two orders of magnitude apart for
  the identical bug.
- Plan: **5-hour session window** (from first message) + **weekly cap** (fixed reset slot per
  account) — shared across *all* Claude surfaces (claude.ai, desktop, Claude Code), not
  per-project. `/usage` and `/context` are the two free commands to check spend; check at the start
  of every session. `/model` — use the default/lighter model for routine implementation, reserve
  the heavier one specifically for arguing through deletion-fixup reasoning. **Agent
  teams/parallel subagents should be OFF** — named as literally "buying the same wrong answer four
  times, concurrently."
- The token-maxing anti-pattern has a short "history" section in the doc making the point that more
  context often makes answers *worse* (buried-middle attention dilution), not just more expensive —
  "a page where everything is highlighted is a page with no highlighting on it at all."
- Bottom line stated directly: **spreading two weeks of work over two weeks fits the allowance
  comfortably; compressing it into one night meets both clocks at once, and only one of them can be
  waited out** (the weekly cap "has no discretion, no sympathy, and no email address").

Not prose — a fixed skeleton per dated entry: `STATE` / `DID` / `DECIDED` (with the one-line *why*)
/ `LEARNED` / `NEXT FIRST STEP` / `OPEN`. The `NEXT FIRST STEP` line is called out as the one that
"pays compound interest" — every session opens by reading it, eliminating the "where was I" restart
tax. Framed as **not extra paperwork but the raw material the required deliverables get smelted
from**: `PROMPTLOG.md` annotation becomes transcription instead of archaeology, `REFLECTION.md` is
half-written before you start it, and the live walkthrough's code-modification task starts from
your own notes instead of zero.

The final section reframes `PROMPTLOG.md` as a genre of document that shows up throughout a real
engineering career (shared/reviewed/inherited transcripts, budget line items, the accountability
trail when something ships broken — "the agent wrote it" is explicitly called out as not being a
valid defense in any real code review, mirroring the spec's "you own the bugs" rule). Practical
instruction: write every prompt as if a senior engineer you respect will read it later, annotate the
log the way you'd annotate a design doc for a teammate (what I asked / what came back / my
judgment and reasons).

  *before* `rb_delete` exists (steal the spec's own Step-4 prompt style). Plan mode + genuinely
  argue with the plan (e.g. "what if the two-children successor is its own right child?"). Record
  the plan revision in `PROMPTLOG.md` *that night*. Implement in slices: two-children reduction,
  then one-child splice, commit at each green rung.
- **Evening 5:** doubly-black case analysis, one case per slice + mirrors, until the table is
  green. Fuzzer with deletes enabled: 10⁵ ops, fixed seed, `rb_validate` every 100 ops, under both
  asan and memcheck. When it fails (it will, at some specific operation number) — **shrink before
  you prompt**. End the evening with a fresh-context adversarial review hunting the spec's named
  bug families (successor-splice use-after-free, overwrite-path key leak, unchecked NULL). Triage
  yourself; log one real finding + one false positive in `PROMPTLOG.md` *tonight* ("doing it Sunday
  from memory takes an hour and reads like fiction").
- **Evening 6:** hardening edge cases (empty tree, single node, overwrite-only-key, whatever the
  devlog's OPEN list accumulated). Finish `PROMPTLOG.md` annotation (transcription from devlog, not
  archaeology) — verify the required 4 episode types are present. Write `REFLECTION.md`. Copy
  remaining transcripts. Check git log ≥8 commits. **Build from a clean clone** to verify the tar
  you'll submit is actually the project you think it is. Stop. If time remains and it's still fun,
  attempt the Reach — but "the buffer comes first. The buffer is load-bearing."

Total lands inside the spec's 8–12 hour estimate *with slack to spare* — explicitly framed as the
difference between a schedule and a gamble.

## Commit discipline

Concrete meaning of "commit wisely": one logical change per commit · commit only from green ·
commit *before* anything risky (so `git restore` — free — is available instead of paying tokens to
have Claude un-write its own recent work, "the saddest line item in this course") · read every
diff before blessing it, test diffs especially (catches the agent quietly weakening a test to make
it pass) · let Claude drive git *conversationally* only after you've already read the diff.

A sample healthy commit log is given (~15 lines from `M0: repo skeleton...` through
`docs: PROMPTLOG episodes 1-5 annotated...`) — useful as a template for what "8+ meaningful
commits" actually looks like in practice, not just in count.

## Testing as a ladder, not a ceremony

Climb one rung per slice, never all-at-once at the end ("the end is where testing goes to become
debugging"):
1. Unit tests born alongside each operation (same evening, not "when the tree is done").
2. `rb_validate` after every mutation inside tests — "the cheapest oracle you own." A bug caught one
   op later is a 5-minute fix; caught 4,000 ops later is an afternoon.
3. Table-driven cases *before* the hard code exists, especially for deletion — a first-draft
   `delete_fixup` will often pass random fuzzing while still failing a targeted case it just never
   randomly encountered.
4. Fuzzer vs. reference model, fixed seeds. On failure: **shrink before you prompt** — a 12-op
   repro is cheap for Claude to debug; a 100,000-op haystack is expensive, "and only one of those
   bills is worth paying."
5. Edge cases nobody fuzzes into by accident: empty tree, single node, overwrite-only-key.

Cadence: `make test` constantly (seconds) · `make asan` after each meaningful change · `make
memcheck` once per evening as a closing ritual (slow — let it be slow at the end, "like dessert").
Two standing rules: **never accept "the tests should pass now"** without real tool output; and
**watch for tests quietly getting weaker** (loosened assertions, vanished cases, thresholds drifting
down) — this is named as a real failure mode of real agents, and your own eyes on every test diff
are the actual enforcement mechanism.

## Debugging loop (the disciplined alternative to "here's my whole codebase, fix it")

The "10:40pm shrug" prompt is explicitly named as failing on both cost *and* effectiveness — it
forces the agent to read everything to answer anything, and a confident multi-file guess-diff
arrives that still has to be reviewed (the work you were trying to skip, just bigger).

Correct loop, in order: **(1) reproduce deterministically** (same seed → same failure every time;
if it won't reproduce, that *is* the bug report — in this assignment nondeterminism almost always
means a read of uninitialized memory or a use-after-free) → **(2) minimize/shrink** the failing
input → **(3) localize** with ASan/valgrind's file+line+backtrace → **(4) prompt scoped to the
module**, naming the file/function, pasting only the relevant tool-output lines (e.g. `grep -A6
'definitely lost'`) → **(5) smallest diff, verify with the same tool, commit, log the episode in
`PROMPTLOG.md` while it's warm**.

**Why brute force ("try again") structurally cannot converge:** every failed attempt stays in
context (cost climbs every turn while progress doesn't) · "try again" adds zero new information ·
the failed attempts become *misleading evidence* the model then conditions on (you're building a
case for the wrong theory) · the code itself degrades underneath you across repeated blind edits.
The exit is unglamorous: Escape, `git restore` to last green, get a deterministic repro, shrink it,
come back with a smaller question and a file name.

## Token/cost mental model (the "why" behind all the above habits)

- A token ≈ 4 chars of English prose, ≈ 3 chars of C source (denser punctuation/identifiers).
- **Input** = everything read (prompt + `CLAUDE.md` + opened files + command output + prior
  replies) — re-sent and re-billed on *every single turn* of a session, not once. "One big file
  read on turn 3 is a purchase. The same file still sitting in context on turn 30 is a
  subscription." **Output** is pricier per-token but input is where volume lives.
- Context window (container size) ≠ usage limit (your budget) — you can be far from filling the
  window and still be out of allowance.
- Two concrete cost scenarios worked out with real numbers: (a) pasting the whole spec into a
  session costs ~30k tokens once, but then gets re-billed on every subsequent message all
  evening — "you paid a fortune to make the answer slightly worse," since it's competing with your
  actual question for the model's attention; (b) "I have a leak, fix it" (~80k tokens/turn,
  compounding, confident 300-line multi-file diff to review) vs. the scoped version from the
  debugging-loop section (~2k tokens/turn, 15-line fix) — roughly two orders of magnitude apart for
  the identical bug.
- Plan: **5-hour session window** (from first message) + **weekly cap** (fixed reset slot per
  account) — shared across *all* Claude surfaces (claude.ai, desktop, Claude Code), not
  per-project. `/usage` and `/context` are the two free commands to check spend; check at the start
  of every session. `/model` — use the default/lighter model for routine implementation, reserve
  the heavier one specifically for arguing through deletion-fixup reasoning. **Agent
  teams/parallel subagents should be OFF** — named as literally "buying the same wrong answer four
  times, concurrently."
- The token-maxing anti-pattern has a short "history" section in the doc making the point that more
  context often makes answers *worse* (buried-middle attention dilution), not just more expensive —
  "a page where everything is highlighted is a page with no highlighting on it at all."
- Bottom line stated directly: **spreading two weeks of work over two weeks fits the allowance
  comfortably; compressing it into one night meets both clocks at once, and only one of them can be
  waited out** (the weekly cap "has no discretion, no sympathy, and no email address").

## The devlog (`DEVLOG.md`) — five minutes, every session, before closing the laptop

Not prose — a fixed skeleton per dated entry: `STATE` / `DID` / `DECIDED` (with the one-line *why*)
/ `LEARNED` / `NEXT FIRST STEP` / `OPEN`. The `NEXT FIRST STEP` line is called out as the one that
"pays compound interest" — every session opens by reading it, eliminating the "where was I" restart
tax. Framed as **not extra paperwork but the raw material the required deliverables get smelted
from**: `PROMPTLOG.md` annotation becomes transcription instead of archaeology, `REFLECTION.md` is
half-written before you start it, and the live walkthrough's code-modification task starts from
your own notes instead of zero.

## Prompt log as a professional artifact (closing reframe)

The final section reframes `PROMPTLOG.md` as a genre of document that shows up throughout a real
engineering career (shared/reviewed/inherited transcripts, budget line items, the accountability
trail when something ships broken — "the agent wrote it" is explicitly called out as not being a
valid defense in any real code review, mirroring the spec's "you own the bugs" rule). Practical
instruction: write every prompt as if a senior engineer you respect will read it later, annotate the
log the way you'd annotate a design doc for a teammate (what I asked / what came back / my
judgment and reasons).

## My standing takeaways for how I (Claude) should apply this companion during the assignment

- When we actually start building, default to the companion's own loop: reread relevant spec
  section → plan mode discussion (and I should push back / ask "what if X" the way the companion
  models, not just accept a plan) → tests first → smallest slice → real tool output before any
  "should work now" claim → commit at green.
- I should actively encourage Nick to keep his own `DEVLOG.md`/`PROMPTLOG.md`/`REFLECTION.md` in
  his own words — the grading explicitly rewards *his* judgment/annotation, and I writing those
  *for* him would undermine the graded artifact and the point of the assignment.
- When debugging together, always push toward a minimal deterministic repro before proposing a fix,
  and always ask for/read actual `make asan`/`make memcheck` output rather than asserting success.
- Be mindful of scope in any exploration I do — name the specific file/function rather than reading
  broadly, in the spirit of both the companion's token guidance and just being a good collaborator.

content.text:
Read both. Here's the shared picture.

## What we're building

A **red-black tree in C**, behind a frozen header you never touch (`include/rbtree.h`). Keys are C strings that **the tree copies and owns**; values are opaque `void *` with an ownership contract you have to get exactly right.

The nine functions: `rb_create`, `rb_insert`, `rb_find`, `rb_delete`, `rb_size`, `rb_foreach` (in-order), `rb_validate`, `rb_destroy`.

Two things make this not a data-structures exercise:

1. **Memory discipline is graded mechanically.** One leaked byte, one invalid read/write, one UB report → that milestone's correctness score is capped at 50%. Verified by `make asan` (ASan+UBSan) *and* `make memcheck` (valgrind), deliberately redundant.
2. **1 of the 5 points is process, not code.** Your raw `.jsonl` transcripts, an annotated `PROMPTLOG.md`, and a **live quiz where you modify your own submitted code from scratch, in front of someone**. Every student sits for it, not a flagged subset.

## The three-allocation rule (the thing most likely to silently sink you)

Every logical node is **three separately-tracked things**:

| Thing | Who frees it | When |
|---|---|---|
| the node struct | tree | delete / destroy |
| the tree's private key copy (`malloc(strlen+1)`) | tree | delete / destroy |
| the `void *value` | depends on the API contract below | — |

The value contract, verbatim in effect:
- `rb_insert` returns **0** → tree now owns `value`, caller must never free it.
- `rb_insert` returns **-1** → ownership **never transferred**, caller still owns it.
- `rb_insert` **overwriting** an existing key → tree frees the *old* value first (it was the only owner).

Rotations move topology only — they never change who owns anything.

## Insert vs. delete, the shape of it

**Insert** breaks Rule 4 (red-red edge). It's local, visible, has an address. New node always goes in red. Red-uncle case = pure recolor, no pointers move, violation relocates two levels up and may repeat. Black uncle = 1–2 rotations, **ceiling of two**, then done.

Two traps flagged hard:
- **Stale root.** If a rotation at the top doesn't update `t->root`, `rb_find` silently searches a subtree and `rb_validate` cheerfully certifies the wrong subtree as legal. The fix is to make `rotate_left`/`rotate_right` themselves own the `t->root` update — and write the regression test the same evening you write the rotations.
- **On the first fixup iteration a black uncle is always NIL.** Real rotation cases only appear after the loop has climbed once — so hand-testing with 5 keys *literally cannot reach them*. That's why the fuzzer is required, not optional polish.

**Delete** breaks Rule 5 (black-height count). It's global, invisible, must be counted. Damage shows up as a "doubly black" deficit — an accounting fiction that lives in your reasoning, **not a third value in your color enum**. Rotation ceiling of three, and every case has a mirror ("the half people forget to write. Or test.").

Two traps here:
- **Two-children case:** hoisting the successor's key means transferring *ownership* of that key allocation. Do it wrong and two nodes both think they own one string → double free at `rb_destroy`.
- **Black node with exactly one child:** that child is provably red. Splice it up, paint it black, done — **no fixup loop at all**. If your code launches the full sibling case analysis here, that's a bug. It's a required explicit test case.
- Standing rule repeated several times: **fixup must never dereference freed memory.** Save what you need before `free()`, or free after fixup. Either order, never the violation.

## Milestones and the grade

| | Work | Pts |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | repo, `CLAUDE.md`, toolchain | — |
| M1 | insert + fixup, find, foreach, validate | 1.5 |
| M2 | delete (all cases) + fuzzer ≥10⁵ ops, green under both tools | 1.5 |
| M3 | hardening, edge cases, clean sweep | 1.0 (quality/memory) |
| | transcripts + live quiz | 1.0 |

`rb_delete` is an honest `return -1;` stub through all of M1. The milestone boundary exists so you're never debugging deletion on top of an insert you don't trust — the spec calls that "an archaeological dig."

Also required: **≥8 meaningful commits** (a single "final submission" commit is an automatic process-grade of **zero**), and copying your `.jsonl` transcripts out periodically — they auto-purge at 30 days.

## Two forward-looking things worth doing on day one

- **Install `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` wrappers immediately** — 4 lines each, just forwarding to malloc/free. That's the seam Assignment 2's fault-injection harness needs. Install it while the house is small.
- **This tree gets reused.** Assignment 2 adds allocators and non-recursive teardown; a near-twin becomes the CFS runqueue in Assignment 4. Nothing here is throwaway.

Recursion in `rb_destroy`/`rb_foreach` is allowed **this assignment only**. Assignment 2 revokes it.

## How I'll work with you

Per the spec's own Section 11 and the companion, and because the grading is built to catch anything else: explore → plan mode → **you argue with the plan** → tests first → smallest slice → real tool output before any "should work now" → adversarial review in fresh context → commit at green. I won't hand you finished implementations, because the live walkthrough is specifically designed to detect that.

Two things stay yours: `DEVLOG.md` / `PROMPTLOG.md` / `REFLECTION.md` are graded on *your* judgment and annotation, and me writing them would defeat the artifact. And when something surprises you mid-build, the reflex order is **spec → your notes → me → a test** — asking me something the spec already answered is buying an answer you already own in print.

---

Where the folder stands: PDFs and notes only. Nothing built yet — no `git init`, no header, no Makefile. That's Evening 1 in the companion's schedule.

Want to start there — repo skeleton, frozen header, starter Makefile, first commit — or do the predict-then-scroll drill on the insertion figures first so the rotation cases are solid before we write any of it?

Found two things before we touch git that change what M0 has to accomplish. Both are toolchain, and M0 *is* toolchain, so this is the right moment.

## The problem: you currently can't detect a leak

The grading rule is "a single leaked byte caps that milestone at 50%," enforced by `make asan` + `make memcheck`. On this machine, neither one can see a leak.

```
==81249==AddressSanitizer: detect_leaks is not supported on this platform.
```

That's real output from your Mac just now. LeakSanitizer doesn't exist on macOS — ASan here catches use-after-free, double-free, and overflows (I verified UAF fires correctly), but **it is structurally blind to leaks**. And valgrind has no Apple Silicon port at all, so `make memcheck` can't run either. You're on `arm64`, no Homebrew, no container runtime.

So of the two independent checks the spec requires, you have about one and a half, and the missing half is exactly the one the harshest grading rule keys on.

**Options, best first:**

1. **Find out if the course has a Linux server.** It's an OS course; there usually is one, and the graders almost certainly run there. Matching the grading environment beats any local setup. Costs you one email or one look at the syllabus. Check this first.
2. **Container runtime locally** (OrbStack or Docker Desktop → an arm64 Linux container). Valgrind and LSan both work there. Then `make memcheck` is real, and you get leak detection back.
3. **Fly blind and hope.** Not viable given the 50% cap.

This does *not* block tonight's skeleton — we write the `memcheck` target now regardless, it just sits unusable until there's a valgrind behind it. But it needs to be solved well before Evening 5, when the fuzzer has to go green under both tools.

Related: `gcc` on your machine is Apple clang wearing a hat, not real GCC. Fine for `-std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror` (I compiled a test clean), but worth knowing the grader may use actual GCC, which warns about slightly different things. A Linux box solves that too.

## Where the repo goes

`Homeworks/hw1/` currently holds the two PDFs and our notes. I'd make the git repo a **subfolder**, not that folder:

```
Homeworks/hw1/
├── CS370-HW1.pdf            ← stays outside the repo
├── CS370-HW1-HowTo.pdf      ← stays outside
├── spec-notes.md            ← stays outside
├── howto-notes.md           ← stays outside
└── rbtree/                  ← git init HERE
    ├── .gitignore
    ├── Makefile
    ├── CLAUDE.md
    ├── DEVLOG.md
    ├── include/rbtree.h     ← FROZEN
    ├── src/rbtree.c
    ├── tests/test_rbtree.c
    ├── tests/fuzz.c
    └── build/               ← gitignored
```

Reason: the submission is a tar of the project, and Evening 6 has you doing a **clean clone** to verify the tar is actually what you think it is. If the PDFs and our notes are inside the repo, that check gets noisy and the tar carries 1MB of course handouts. Keeping the repo root pure means the clean clone tests exactly the thing being graded.

One consequence worth naming: you'll then have two `CLAUDE.md` files in scope — the course brain at `CS 370/CLAUDE.md` and the project one at `rbtree/CLAUDE.md`. Both load every turn, both get billed every turn. The project one stays **lean**: build/test commands, the frozen-header rule, the code map, "smallest change that passes." Not an essay.

## Tonight's sequence

Four steps, two or three commits. All boring on purpose.

**1. Skeleton + `git init`** — directories, `.gitignore` (`build/`, `*.o`, binaries, `.DS_Store`), empty-but-present source files. Commit #1 has no working code in it, and that's correct.

**2. The frozen header** goes into `include/rbtree.h`, untouched from here to submission. This is the one thing I can't do for you — see below.

**3. The Makefile.** Targets: `all`, `test`, `asan`, `memcheck`, `clean`. Two build dirs (`build/` and `build/asan/`) because the object files differ — mixing instrumented and uninstrumented objects produces confusing garbage. I'd also put the **`rb_malloc`/`rb_free` wrappers in from the start**, four lines each forwarding to malloc/free. That's the seam Assignment 2's fault injector needs, and installing it now costs nothing while the file is empty.

**4. A compiling stub `src/rbtree.c`** — every one of the nine functions present and honest (`rb_delete` returns `-1`, `rb_find` returns `NULL`, etc.). This matters because "commit at green" needs a green to commit at. A skeleton that builds clean under `-Werror` is a real baseline; a skeleton that doesn't compile is a liability you'll debug on Evening 2 while trying to think about node structs.

Then `/init`-style hand-editing of `CLAUDE.md`, commit, and the rest of the evening is the exploration session — questions only, zero edits, working through whatever the spec left you unsure about.

Notice `rb_insert` isn't in that list. Evening 1 writes no algorithm. That's the schedule working as designed.

## What's actually yours to decide

Three things I'm not going to quietly pick for you, because two of them are plausible walkthrough questions:

- **Parent pointers or not.** The spec calls this "your first real design decision." Textbook fixup algorithms assume one; the cost is another pointer to keep correct through every rotation. This gets settled Evening 2 with the reason written into `DEVLOG.md`, not tonight.
- **NULL-as-black vs. an explicit sentinel NIL node.** Affects how much special-casing lives in your fixup code.
- **The repo subfolder name.** I used `rbtree/` above; call it whatever you want.

## What I need from you to start

**Blocking:** the exact text of the frozen header. I can't read the PDFs — no poppler, and no Homebrew to install it with. Open `CS370-HW1.pdf`, find the `rbtree.h` block, and paste it here. Copy-paste beats me transcribing from a page render anyway: this file has to be byte-for-byte what they gave you, and it's a graded deliverable.

**Not blocking, but worth doing this week:** installing Homebrew would unlock poppler (so I can read lecture PDFs all semester instead of asking you to paste), plus real GCC. Separate from the container/Linux question above.

**Housekeeping:** your transcripts are at `~/.claude/projects/-Users-nicholasmarechal-Desktop-CS-370/` — two sessions so far, 28MB from the spec-reading one. Those auto-purge at 30 days and they're a graded deliverable. Copy them somewhere safe tonight and make it a weekly habit. One caveat: that folder name is derived from the directory Claude Code was launched in, so if you later start sessions from inside `rbtree/`, transcripts land in a *different* folder. Check both before you submit.

Paste the header and I'll lay out the exact skeleton — you read it before anything gets written.

content.text:
Good questions — the SSH one is more consequential than it looks. Let me take them in order.

## GitHub: no, you don't need one

I grepped both notes for `github`, `gitlab`, `classroom`, `origin`, `push` — **zero hits.** The submission path is a **tar uploaded to Canvas**, and the companion's Evening 1 opens with "empty repo, `git init`" — if the class provided a repo, that line would say *clone*. The Evening 6 "clean clone" check also works fine against a local path (`git clone ./rbtree /tmp/verify`).

So: `git init`, local, done. The ≥8 commits requirement is about your local history, which travels inside the tar via the `.git` directory.

One caveat on my confidence: my notes are a compression of a 40-page PDF, so if there's a submission-logistics line I squeezed out, Canvas is the place to confirm. But two independent documents both describing a local-init workflow is strong evidence.

**That said** — I'd still put a **private GitHub repo on it as backup.** Not for credit. The repo *is* the graded artifact, school machines get wiped, and laptops die in week 2 of a two-week assignment. It also turns out to be the cleanest Mac↔Linux transport if you go hybrid below. Costs nothing, doesn't change the tar.

## The real question your SSH comment raises

Here's the thing that needs deciding tonight, before there's any history to migrate:

**Claude Code's session transcripts are written on whatever machine Claude Code runs on.** Those `.jsonl` files are a graded deliverable worth 0.5 points. In a VS Code Remote-SSH window, the integrated terminal runs *on the remote* — so `claude` launched there writes its transcripts to the Linux box's `~/.claude/projects/`, not your Mac's.

Get this wrong and by Evening 5 you have six sessions split across two machines, some already past the 30-day purge window. So "where do I work" isn't a comfort preference here — it's "where does a graded deliverable get written."

Three shapes this can take:

**A — Everything on the Linux box.** Repo, builds, and Claude Code all remote; VS Code Remote-SSH is just your editor.
- Every tool works: valgrind runs, real GCC, and **ASan on Linux enables leak detection by default** — so `make asan` starts catching leaks immediately, no flags needed. The thing your Mac cannot do at all.
- Matches the grading environment. GCC's `-Werror` set isn't identical to clang's; you don't want to meet that difference at submission time.
- One machine, one transcript folder, one thing to remember to copy.
- Cost: installing and authenticating Claude Code on the remote (needs Node). One-time, Evening 1 — which is exactly where toolchain costs belong.

**B — All on the Mac, SSH only to run memcheck.** Simple, transcripts local, but leak detection is out of your daily loop — and that's the rule that caps you at 50%. You'd only find leaks when you remembered to sync and go look.

**C — Hybrid, GitHub as the wire.** Develop on Mac, push, pull on Linux, run the battery there. The companion does prescribe `make memcheck` as a once-per-evening closing ritual, so a nightly remote run genuinely fits the intended cadence. Still weaker than A: leaks surface hours after you write them instead of immediately.

**I'd go with A** if that Linux box is reliably up and yours to use. The single strongest argument: the tool enforcing the harshest grading rule should run in your normal edit-build-test loop, not in a separate ritual you might skip on a tired evening.

### Probe the box before committing to it

SSH in and run this — it answers whether A is actually viable:

```bash
uname -m; git --version; gcc --version | head -1; echo 'int main(void){return 0;}' > /tmp/t.c && gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror /tmp/t.c -o /tmp/t && echo "c23 OK"; valgrind --version || echo "NO valgrind"; node --version || echo "NO node"
```

Paste me the output. What I'm looking for: does GCC there actually accept `-std=c23` (older GCC wants `-std=c2x`, which would change the Makefile), is valgrind present, and is Node available for Claude Code. Also worth a glance at your disk quota if it's a shared server — transcripts get large, your current one is already 28MB.

## On following the how-to for full credit

One correction worth making now, because it affects what "full credit" means.

The companion **is not the grading contract.** By its own framing it "never overrides the spec — where they'd seem to disagree, the spec wins," and it's "not required reading for the grade directly." It's the recommended *working method*, and the professor notes that students who land at the top of the transcript rubric tend to work that way anyway.

The **spec** holds the things you can lose points for: the nine functions, the ownership contract, ≥10⁵ fuzz ops, `rb_validate` every 100 ops, the required targeted deletion cases, ≥8 commits, the 4–6 annotated `PROMPTLOG.md` episodes, the raw transcripts.

So: **companion for rhythm, spec as the checklist.** You could follow the companion flawlessly and still drop a point by missing a spec threshold. Before submission we walk the spec's deliverables list line by line and check each one off against the actual repo. I'll keep the companion's loop as our default working style — that part's already in how I'm operating.

## Where that leaves us

Decision order matters: **pick the machine first, then build the skeleton there.** Creating it on the Mac and moving it later means migrating a `.git` directory and splitting your transcripts across two hosts — avoidable by choosing now.

Two things from you:

1. **Run the probe** on the Linux box and paste the output — or tell me it's not reliably available and we plan around the Mac.
2. **The frozen header text**, still blocking. Open `CS370-HW1.pdf`, find the `rbtree.h` block, paste it. Copy-paste beats me transcribing a page render, and this file has to be exactly what they gave you.

Once I have both, I'll lay out the full skeleton — every file, every Makefile target — for you to read and argue with before a single thing gets written.

## What the header locks in

Reading it closely, four things are decided *for* us:

- **`typedef struct rbtree rbtree_t;` with no definition** — the opaque type. Both `struct rbtree` and your node struct live inside `src/rbtree.c`, invisible to any test file. Your tests can only touch the nine public functions, same as the grader.
- **`const rbtree_t *` on find/size/foreach/validate** — those four promise not to mutate. Free to honor now, annoying if you later want lazy caching.
- **`0` means success everywhere** — `rb_insert`, `rb_delete`, and `rb_validate` all return 0 for good, nonzero for bad. Inverted from a boolean, and easy to write backwards once.
- **`rb_find` returns NULL for absent** — which means it *cannot distinguish* "no such key" from "key present, value is NULL." That ambiguity is baked into the frozen API, so it isn't your bug — but don't write a test that assumes otherwise.

Only `<stddef.h>`, only for `size_t`.

Three separately-owned things per node: the node, the tree's private key
copy, and the caller's `void *value`.
